title: Battles view: unscrollable side lists, empty assassinations, split routs
description:
# Summary

The battles view (`BattlesDialog`, delivered by ah-1is.2 in PR #173) has five defects that make
larger and unusual battles unreadable. Reported by the navigator from a real turn report.

# The defects

1. **The ATTACKERS and DEFENDERS lists do not scroll.** Past roughly ten entries per side the rows
   are compressed on top of each other instead of the list scrolling, and the side becomes
   unreadable. Each list needs its own scroll region with a sane minimum row height.

2. **Outcome is below the rounds.** The outcome section should come *before* the round-by-round
   detail — it is what the reader wants first, and the rounds are the supporting detail.

3. **Assassinations render almost empty.** An assassination shows no attackers and no defenders,
   and the outcome shows only the bare word "Casualties" with nothing after it. Expected:
   - Attackers: when the assassin is unknown (as it is for the victim's faction), show `?`.
   - Defenders: show the assassinated unit.
   - Outcome: the actual casualties, not a bare heading.

4. **The right-hand panel keeps its scroll position across battles.** Switching to another battle in
   the list should always start the detail panel back at the top; today it stays wherever the
   previous battle was scrolled to, so a new battle can open mid-way down.

5. **A rout is parsed as a separate battle.** When a side is routed the rout appears as its own
   entry in the battle list instead of being folded into the battle it came from. The rout belongs
   to the originating battle.

# Scope

- `packages/shared/src/workspace/BattlesDialog.tsx` — 1, 2, 3 (rendering), 4
- `packages/shared/src/workspace/battles.ts` — 3 (assassination shape), 5 (rout grouping)
- `crates/core/src/report/battle.rs` — only if the assassination/rout defects turn out to originate
  in the parser rather than in the TS layer; check before changing it.

# Out of scope

- Any redesign of the battles view beyond these five fixes.
- New battle information not already present in the report.

# Validation

- `pnpm test` (or the workspace's test task) covering `battles.test.ts` and `BattlesDialog.test.tsx`
- Manual: open a turn report containing (a) a battle with more than ten units per side,
  (b) an assassination, (c) a battle ending in a rout; confirm each renders as described above.
acceptance_criteria: Attacker and defender lists scroll independently and stay readable past ten entries; the outcome section renders above the rounds; an assassination shows ? for an unknown attacker, the assassinated unit as defender, and real casualties in the outcome; selecting another battle resets the detail panel to the top; a rout appears inside its originating battle rather than as a separate battle

title: Skip CI for docs-only PRs
description:
PRs that only touch files under docs/ currently trigger the full CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml) — wasm build, JS checks, Rust checks, Playwright smoke/pwa suites, and the native Tauri e2e job. None of these depend on documentation content, so a docs-only PR waits on the same ~10+ minute pipeline as a code change before it can be merged, even though nothing it changed can affect the outcome.

This bead is about making docs-only PRs quickly mergeable: when a PR's diff is confined to docs/, CI should not need to run (or should complete near-instantly) to satisfy branch protection.
design:
## Context

A PR that touches only `docs/` waits on the whole of `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the wasm build,
the JS checks, the Rust job, four sharded Playwright runs, the PWA run, a macOS compile and the
Linux native end-to-end suite — before it can merge. Nothing in it can be affected by a documentation
change. The planning role produces such PRs routinely (the mockup PRs, #152 and #153), so this is
paid several times a week.

The `main` ruleset requires ten status checks by name, and they are:

    checks · rust · wasm · pwa · native · desktop-shell
    smoke (web, 1, 2) · smoke (web, 2, 2) · smoke (desktop-shell, 1, 2) · smoke (desktop-shell, 2, 2)

with `strict_required_status_checks_policy: true`, so the branch must also be up to date with main.
All ten must report; the ruleset is not to be edited by this bead.

**The mechanism is documented, and the two cases are opposite.** GitHub's *Troubleshooting required
status checks*:

> If a workflow is skipped due to path filtering, branch filtering or a commit message, then checks
> associated with that workflow will remain in a "Pending" state. A pull request that requires those
> checks to be successful will be blocked from merging.
>
> If, however, a job within a workflow is skipped due to a conditional, it will report its status as
> "Success".

and successful statuses are `success`, `skipped` and `neutral`. So the workflow must keep running on
every pull request, and the *jobs* inside it are what a docs-only diff skips. `paths-ignore` is the
trap, not the tool.

When this lands: a docs-only PR is mergeable in about a minute, and everything else runs exactly as
it does today.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

- **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`**:
  - `on: pull_request` keeps **no** `paths` or `paths-ignore`. That is load-bearing; see the quote
    above.
  - A new first job, `changes`, whose single output `code` says whether anything outside `docs/`
    was touched. It needs no checkout and no toolchain: `gh api
    repos/${{ github.repository }}/pulls/${{ github.event.number }}/files --paginate --jq
    '.[].filename'`, and `code=true` unless every line begins `docs/`. `gh` is preinstalled on the
    runners; `GITHUB_TOKEN` goes in the step's env.
  - On anything that is not a `pull_request` — the push to main — `code` is `true` without asking.
  - `if: needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'` on `wasm`, `checks`, `rust`, `smoke`, `pwa`,
    `desktop-shell` and `native`, adding `changes` to each `needs` (the three that already have
    `needs: wasm` become `needs: [changes, wasm]`).
  - The workflow has no `permissions:` block, so it takes the repository default. If that default is
    not enough for `pulls: read`, add `permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: read }` at the
    workflow level rather than widening anything.
- **`scripts/ciDocsGate.test.ts`** — new, under `test:tooling`. This repository already tests its own
  configuration this way: `scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts` reads `.cargo/config.toml` and asserts
  the properties that would break elsewhere. Same shape here, over `ci.yml`.
- **`README.md`**, the CI section if it describes the workflow's jobs — one sentence that a docs-only
  PR skips them.

**No new dependency.** `dorny/paths-filter` is the usual answer and is named in the bead as an
example; `gh api` needs no third-party action to audit or pin, and the rule it implements is three
lines of shell. Nothing else in this workflow uses a third-party action beyond the official
`actions/*`, `dtolnay/rust-toolchain`, `Swatinem/rust-cache` and `pnpm/action-setup` it already has.

## Increments

1. **The invariant, before the change.** RED: `scripts/ciDocsGate.test.ts` —
   `every required job is gated on the docs check` fails, because no job is. GREEN: the `changes`
   job and the seven `if:` lines.
2. **The trap, pinned.** RED: `the pull request trigger carries no path filter`. It passes the
   moment it is written, which is the point — it exists so a later "simplification" to `paths-ignore`
   fails here instead of silently leaving every required check Pending for ever. Say so in the
   commit; do not manufacture a failing state for it.
3. **The real thing.** Verified on GitHub, not in a test. See Validation.

## The test plan

Suite: `pnpm run test:tooling`. Nothing else can reach a workflow file.

`scripts/ciDocsGate.test.ts`, reading `.github/workflows/ci.yml` as text:
- `every required job is gated on the docs check` — for each of `wasm`, `checks`, `rust`, `smoke`,
  `pwa`, `desktop-shell`, `native`, that job's block carries
  `if: needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'`. This is the test that catches the eighth job somebody
  adds next year and forgets to gate.
- `the gate job is not one of the required checks` — `changes` is not in the required list, so it
  must not be gated on itself and must not be renamed to collide with a required context.
- `the pull request trigger carries no path filter` — no `paths:` or `paths-ignore:` under
  `on.pull_request`.
- `the gate runs everything when the diff cannot be read` — assert the shell in the job defaults to
  `code=true`, by asserting the fallback is present rather than by running it. The direction matters
  more than the mechanism: a gate that fails closed skips CI, which is the one outcome worse than
  slow CI.

Parse by scanning lines rather than by adding a YAML dependency — the file is uniformly two-space
indented and the job ids sit at exactly two spaces. Keep the assertions few and specific; see the
traps.

## User-facing decisions

None. This is CI configuration; the application has no part in it, and nothing a player sees
changes.

Two judgements taken here rather than left open: the gate is `gh api` rather than a third-party
paths-filter action (no dependency to pin, three lines of shell), and the ten required contexts in
the `main` ruleset are left exactly as they are — the whole design exists so that they keep
reporting.

## Out of scope

- Editing the `main` ruleset, or the set of required checks.
- `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and `release.yml`. A docs merge to main will still deploy; whether
  it should is a separate question with a different risk attached.
- Widening the rule beyond `docs/` — root `*.md`, `.beads/issues.jsonl`, `LICENSE`. The bead says
  `docs/`, and each addition is a place where a real change could slip through ungated. If the
  navigator wants more later, it is a one-line change with its own conversation.
- Speeding up CI for code PRs.
- The `strict` policy that requires a branch to be up to date with main.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run test:tooling
pnpm run check
```

Then on GitHub, which is the only place this can actually be proved. The bead's own PR touches
`.github/` and `scripts/`, so it must show the **full** suite running — that is half the acceptance
criteria, free.

For the other half, open a throwaway PR from a branch that changes one line of a file under `docs/`
and confirm:

- all ten required contexts report, none stays Pending, and the merge box goes green in about a
  minute;
- **the four matrix contexts appear** — `smoke (web, 1, 2)` and its three siblings. This is the one
  part that documentation does not settle (see the traps), and it is the reason this trial is
  mandatory rather than a nicety;
- then push a code change onto the same branch and confirm every job runs, proving a mixed diff is
  not skipped.

Close the throwaway PR without merging. Do not merge this bead until that trial has been run and its
result stated in the PR description.

## Known traps

- **`paths-ignore` is the failure mode, not the fix.** A workflow skipped by path filtering leaves
  its required checks Pending for ever and blocks the PR — GitHub documents exactly this. The
  workflow must keep triggering on every pull request; only its jobs are conditional. The test in
  increment 2 exists to keep that from being "tidied up" later.
- **Four of the ten contexts are generated by the matrix.** A skipped matrix job is expected to
  still produce one skipped check run per combination, but that is the piece the documentation does
  not state outright. If the trial PR shows those four staying Pending, the fallback is a twin job
  with the *same* `name:` and the *same* matrix, gated the other way
  (`if: needs.changes.outputs.code != 'true'`) and doing nothing but `echo`. Take that route only if
  the trial demands it — two check runs with one name is a wrinkle worth avoiding when it is not
  needed.
- **A job cannot read `needs.changes.outputs` unless `changes` is in its `needs`.** The three jobs
  that already declare `needs: wasm` are the easy ones to get wrong, and the failure is quiet: an
  unresolvable `needs.*` expression evaluates to empty, the `if` is false, and the job silently
  never runs on any PR at all.
- **Fail open, always.** If the API call fails, the diff cannot be read, or the event is anything
  other than a pull request, `code` must be `true`. A gate that fails closed turns an API blip into
  a merged, untested change.
- **The gate job must not be named after a required context**, and must not be added to the ruleset.
  It reports its own check named `changes`, which nothing requires.
- **`strict_required_status_checks_policy` is on**, so a docs PR that has fallen behind main still
  needs updating from main before it merges. That is a push, so the gate re-runs — cheaply. Do not
  try to solve that here.
- **Line-scanning a YAML file is brittle.** Assert on the few properties that matter and anchor them
  to the two-space job indentation; a test that tries to reimplement YAML will fail on the next
  comment reflow and be deleted by whoever it annoys.
- **Do not `git checkout main`** — another agent usually holds it in a worktree. Branch from
  `origin/main` after `git fetch origin main`.
acceptance_criteria:
- A PR whose diff touches only files under docs/ can be merged without waiting on the full CI job matrix (wasm/checks/rust/smoke/pwa/desktop-shell/native).
- Branch protection's required status checks still pass for docs-only PRs — i.e. this is not accomplished by making checks optional, since GitHub does not satisfy a required check that never ran. Use path filtering that still reports a (fast/no-op) success status for the required check names, e.g. via dorny/paths-filter with a lightweight fallback job, rather than relying on paths-ignore alone.
- A PR that touches docs/ together with any non-docs file still runs the full CI suite as today.
- Existing CI behavior for non-docs PRs is unchanged (same jobs, same triggers, same required checks).

title: An implementer running under the launcher can be neither watched nor reached
description:
ah-6xq.10 shipped `scripts/run-implementer` running `claude --print --verbose`, and documented two
things about it that are false. Both were verified wrong straight after the merge:

- **`--print` in text format prints only the final message.** A 45-second probe produced one line.
  `--verbose` has no effect on text output, so an hour-long bead shows nothing until it ends.
  `orchestrator.md` and the bead plan claim it "streams its work to the terminal".
- **A `--print` session does not appear in `claude agents --json` or `ListAgents`**, so `SendMessage`
  cannot reach it. `orchestrator.md` and CLAUDE.md claim terminal sessions stay reachable as peers -
  that was verified on an interactive session and does not hold in print mode.

So Cerebro has no way to see what an implementer is doing, and the navigator watching the terminal
sees nothing until the bead is finished.
design:
`--output-format stream-json --verbose` does stream live - each `tool_use` with its tool name, each
result, and the assistant text, confirmed by probe. The fix is that flag plus somewhere to put the
stream:

- the terminal gets readable lines through a small pure formatter, so the navigator can watch;
- the raw JSONL is tee'd to `.claude/implementers/<name>.log`, which gives Cerebro something to read
  and replaces the SendMessage channel that does not exist.

Then correct every document that claims otherwise.
acceptance_criteria:
- The launcher runs claude with --output-format stream-json and renders readable lines to the terminal.
- The raw stream is written to .claude/implementers/<name>.log for the orchestrator to read.
- A malformed or non-JSON line never crashes the launcher.
- orchestrator.md, implementer.md and CLAUDE.md no longer claim an implementer is reachable by
  SendMessage or that text mode streams the work.

title: Implementers run as their own sessions, one bead per process
description:
## Problem

Observed live during the first orchestrator test run (Cerebro + implementer Cyclops, ah-f8u):
after opening PR #161 and requesting the Copilot review, Cyclops's own agent turn ended with
"I'll wait now for the monitor's event" — it had armed a Monitor (or similar wait) for the
review to land, and yielded rather than blocking. The review landed a couple of minutes later,
but nothing woke Cyclops back up: it dropped out of the agent list entirely, left two review
comments unanswered, and the bead sat in_progress with an expired lease until Cerebro noticed
and manually resumed it via SendMessage.

The same shape happened earlier in the same run for a genuine stall (a hung wasm build), which
is a different failure mode (harness killed it after a 600s stalled-stream watchdog) but has the
same symptom: the implementer stops with a bead still open and nothing brings it back except a
human or the orchestrator noticing and manually resuming it.

## Scope (for /plan-bead to work out)

Make the implementer either:
- never yield/end its turn while a bead's PR is open and unmerged (poll/block instead of arming
  a Monitor and ending its turn), or
- ensure whatever wait mechanism it uses reliably re-invokes the implementer itself when the
  awaited event fires, not just notifies the orchestrator, or
- have the implementer treat "PR open, not yet merged, bead not closed" as a state it must
  actively return to and verify before it is allowed to consider a work cycle finished — so even
  if it stops for any reason, the orchestrator's routine check-in has a documented, expected
  recovery step to resume it (this may already be partly true - the gap is that nothing currently
  prompts the resume automatically).

Also worth deciding: what should happen for the harder case (the 600s stall-kill) versus the
softer case (turn ended cleanly while waiting) - they may need different handling.

## Context

Full incident detail is in the Cerebro/navigator conversation from 2026-08-13 (the first
orchestrator dry run). Cerebro's own agent instructions and the implement-bead skill are the
likely places to change; this bead intentionally leaves the approach open for planning.

## Out of scope

Changing anything about the Copilot review policy itself, or about the wasm build/CI setup.
design:
## Context

An implementer was a **subagent**, and a subagent has no next turn: when it emits its final text the
`Agent` call returns and the session is gone. Every asynchronous wait the harness offers — `Monitor`,
`Bash` with `run_in_background` — is built on "keep working, the notification re-invokes you later",
which cannot hold for something that has already ended. Cyclops armed one against PR #161's review,
said "I'll wait now for the monitor's event", and ended its turn. The review landed two minutes later
with nobody left to receive it: two comments unanswered, the bead `in_progress` with an expiring
lease, and no recovery until Cerebro noticed and resumed it by hand. The same shape had already
happened once that run, when the harness killed a stalled implementer on its 600s watchdog.

**The fix is to stop making implementers subagents.** An implementer becomes its own top-level Claude
session, started by a launcher script in a terminal of its own. A top-level session can wait — it can
block inside a tool call, and nothing about its lifecycle depends on a parent staying alive. The loop
that used to live inside the agent's context moves into the launcher: one `claude` process per bead,
started fresh, exiting when the bead is merged, and relaunched by the script for as long as the
navigator's go flag is set. So "one bead per process" (ah-6xq.8) stops being a discipline the agent
has to keep and becomes a fact of how it is run, and context can no longer grow across beads.

Cerebro keeps control without spawning anything: it writes the flags the launcher reads, and — because
these are peer sessions rather than subagents — it can also `SendMessage` them directly.

Verified while planning, in this session, so none of it has to be rediscovered:

- `claude --agent implementer --name Cyclops` starts a top-level session; `--print --verbose` streams
  its work to the terminal so the navigator can watch it; the process exits when the run is done,
  which is what lets a shell loop own the cadence.
- `claude agents --json` lists live sessions with name, status, pid and cwd.
- A bounded foreground `until <cond>; do ...; sleep N; done` blocks a turn and returns — the wait
  mechanism this design relies on, available today.
- **A `--bg` session is invisible to `ListAgents` and therefore cannot be reached by `SendMessage`,
  while a terminal session is visible.** This is why the launcher runs in a terminal: it keeps
  Cerebro's second control channel, and it is the opposite of what the flag's name suggests.
- The `claude attach|logs|stop <id>` hints printed by `--bg` are **not subcommands in 2.1.231** and
  run as prompts if typed. Do not build on them.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

- **`scripts/runImplementer.ts`** (new) — the launcher. Pure decision functions plus a thin loop,
  following `scripts/gateLock.ts`: predicates take their inputs as arguments, the clock is passed in,
  process wiring stays at the bottom. `scripts/prune-worktrees.sh` is the other precedent for an
  agent-facing script, and its `--watch` loop is the shape of this one's idle poll.
- **`scripts/runImplementer.test.ts`** (new) — vitest, run by `pnpm run test:tooling` via
  `vitest.tooling.config.ts`. Model it on `scripts/gateLock.test.ts`, including its habit of saying in
  the test body why a case matters.
- **`.claude/agents/implementer.md`** — rewritten. It is a top-level session, it does exactly one
  bead, it exits when that bead is merged, and it never checks a stop flag mid-run because the
  launcher owns the loop now.
- **`.claude/skills/implement-bead/SKILL.md`** — "Being told to stop" and the loop at the end of
  "Finishing, then going again" go away; the wait discipline replaces the bare "Then wait for it".
- **`.claude/agents/orchestrator.md`** — no more `Agent` spawning. Control is the flag files, plus
  `SendMessage` to a named peer; observation is `claude agents --json` and `ListAgents`. The claim
  sweep added in PR #160 stays as it is.
- **`CLAUDE.md`** (edit `.github/copilot-instructions.md`; `CLAUDE.md` is a symlink to it) — the
  orchestration section describes the new topology.

Reuse `bd heartbeat` rather than inventing a keepalive, and the `gh` selectors already in
`implement-bead` and `CLAUDE.md`.

## Increments

1. **The flag decision.** RED: `runImplementer.test.ts` — "launches while the go flag is set", "idles
   when it is absent", "exits on the stop flag", "stop wins over go when both are present", against
   `nextAction({ go, stop })` returning `"launch" | "idle" | "exit"`. GREEN: implement in
   `runImplementer.ts`.
2. **The flag paths.** RED: "puts an implementer's flags under .claude/implementers/<name>" and
   "rejects a name that would escape that directory" against `flagPaths(name)` — a name reaching the
   filesystem needs the traversal case pinned, not assumed.
3. **The launcher loop.** RED: spawn `tsx scripts/runImplementer.ts <name>` with a stubbed `claude`
   on `PATH` (`gateLock.test.ts` already spawns real processes, so the cost is established) and
   assert: it invokes `claude` once per iteration while the go flag is set; it invokes it again after
   the first exits; it stops invoking when the flag is removed; it exits on the stop flag and removes
   it. Also assert **the command line it builds** — `--agent implementer --name <name> --print
   --verbose` — since that is the contract with the terminal the navigator is watching.
4. **The documents.** No test; prose. `implementer.md`, then the skill, then `orchestrator.md`, then
   `CLAUDE.md`. Last, so they describe a launcher that exists.

## The test plan

`scripts/runImplementer.test.ts`, vitest, tooling suite only:

- `nextAction` — launch / idle / exit; stop beats go; neither flag means idle.
- `flagPaths` — the two paths for a name; rejects `..` and a name containing a slash.
- The loop, spawned with a stubbed `claude` that records its argv: relaunches after an exit while go
  is set; stops when go is removed mid-run; exits and clears the flag on stop; passes the expected
  argv.

**Suites to run: `pnpm run lint`, `pnpm run typecheck`, `pnpm run test:tooling`.** No browser suite is
involved — nothing here is reachable from the app bundle — and running smoke or PWA would take the
machine-wide gate lock for no signal.

What no unit test can show is that a real implementer session completes a real bead and exits.
Validation covers that.

## User-facing decisions

Two, both taken with the navigator during planning; neither has a UI surface, so there is no mockup.

1. **Implementers are launched by the navigator, one terminal each**, rather than by Cerebro with
   `--bg`. Chosen for visibility, and because a `--bg` session cannot be reached by `SendMessage`
   (verified above), so a terminal session is in fact the *more* controllable of the two.
2. **A go flag authorises continued work, one bead at a time.** The agent does one bead and exits;
   the launcher re-reads the flag and starts a fresh one. Removing the flag lets the current bead
   finish and stops the next launch.

## Out of scope

- **The Copilot review policy.** One review per PR, requested on open, never re-requested, twenty
  minutes then escalate. Unchanged.
- **The wasm build hang** behind the original 600s stall-kill. A real defect, a different bead.
- **Cerebro launching implementers unattended.** Explicitly decided against; do not add a `--bg`
  path "for convenience".
- **Any change to CI, the gate lock, the ports, or the claim sweep from PR #160.**

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run lint
pnpm run typecheck
pnpm run test:tooling
```

Then the end-to-end check, which is the point of the bead and which only a human can judge:

1. In a terminal: `scripts/run-implementer <name>` with the go flag set, against a real planned bead.
2. Watch it take the bead, open the PR, wait for the review **without ending its run**, answer the
   comments, rebase, wait for CI, merge, close the bead, and exit.
3. Confirm the launcher then starts a second session for the next bead, and that removing the go flag
   mid-bead lets that bead finish and stops the next launch.
4. Confirm `bd show <bead>` shows a lease that was renewed across the CI wait rather than expiring.

## Known traps

- **`--print` mode ends when the model stops.** In-turn blocking is therefore the only wait that is
  guaranteed to work: `Monitor` and background `Bash` promise a later re-invocation this process may
  not be alive for. Wait with a bounded foreground loop and nothing else.
- **Silence gets a run killed.** The harness has a 600s stalled-stream watchdog and it has already
  killed an implementer here. Any wait loop must print each poll, and no single `Bash` call may
  approach ten minutes — its own timeout maxes at 600000ms and defaults to 120000ms. A twenty-minute
  review wait is three calls, not one.
- **Heartbeat inside the wait, not around it.** A five-minute lease does not survive a ten-minute CI
  wait, so the loop body carries `bd heartbeat <id>` — `until <cond>; do bd heartbeat <id>; sleep 30;
  done`. A heartbeat before and after the wait leaves the middle uncovered.
- **`bd` resolves its workspace from the working directory**, so the heartbeat must run with a cwd
  inside the repository.
- **Never `cd` into another agent's worktree.** The shell keeps its directory between calls, and one
  stray `cd` sends every later git command somewhere else.
- **`git checkout main` fails while another worktree holds it.** Branch from `origin/main`.
- **The launcher must not relaunch after a failed run in a tight loop.** A `claude` that exits
  immediately — bad flag, no auth — would otherwise spin. Back off and say so.
- **A stop flag left behind stops the next session too**, which is why the launcher removes it as it
  exits, exactly as the old in-agent check did.

title: An orchestrator that starts and stops implementer subagents
description:
## Summary

Replace the process-per-bead loop (ah-6xq.8, merged as #156) with an interactive orchestrator
session that spins implementer subagents up and down on command.

## Why the previous approach is being withdrawn

ah-6xq.8 moved the loop out of the session so each bead started with a clean context, and named each
session so it could be reached over Remote Control. Remote Control did not work in practice, and
without it a `claude -p` loop is a black box: it cannot be inspected, redirected or stopped short of
killing the process.

## What replaces it

- `/implement-bead` loops again — bead after bead — until it is told to stop.
- An **orchestrator** session, interactive, on Sonnet, that starts and stops implementer subagents on
  the navigator's command and launches nothing on its own.
- Implementers run as subagents on Sonnet in auto mode, each with its own context.
- **Taking one down means telling it to finish**: it completes the bead it is on, sees it merged to
  main, and only then leaves the loop. Nothing is killed mid-bead, because a half-done bead leaves a
  claim, a worktree and an open PR behind.

## Scope

- An orchestrator agent definition, and the instructions it runs on.
- An implementer agent definition running the `implement-bead` skill.
- The stop protocol, checked at the one safe point in the loop: after a merge, before the next claim.
- Revert the parts of #156 that made a session stop after one bead, and remove
  `scripts/implement-loop.sh`.
- Update `docs/agent-workflow.md`, which is the human's guide and still describes the pre-#156 world.

## Out of scope

- Anything inside a bead: claiming, TDD, review, merge, cleanup are unchanged.
- The planning role, which stays interactive and unlooped.
- Reviving Remote Control.

## Note on context

An implementer that loops many beads accumulates context again — the problem #156 addressed. Under
this design that is managed by hand instead: the navigator takes an implementer down and brings a
fresh one up, which is a deliberate lever rather than an automatic one.
acceptance_criteria: implement-bead loops until told to stop; an orchestrator agent on Sonnet starts and stops implementer subagents only when asked; implementers run on Sonnet in auto mode with their own context; a stopped implementer finishes and merges its current bead before leaving the loop; scripts/implement-loop.sh is gone and docs/agent-workflow.md describes the new arrangement

title: One bead per process: move the implementer's loop out of its context
description:
## Problem

`implement-bead` ends with "Then pick up the next planned bead", so one session builds bead after
bead in one context. The context therefore grows without bound: every finished bead's diffs, test
output, CI watches and review threads stay in the window while the next bead is built. Auto-compaction
only summarises it, which keeps a lossy trace of finished work instead of a clean slate.

An agent cannot clear its own context. `/clear` is a built-in CLI command the user types, and the
Skill tool does not invoke built-in commands. So the loop has to live outside the process.

## Why this is cheap

Nothing needs to survive between beads. Every piece of state the implementer carries forward lives
in bd (the claim, the labels, the plan in `design`) or in git (main, the PR). The conversation holds
nothing bead N+1 needs, which is what makes a fresh process per bead free rather than a workaround.

## Scope

- A loop script that runs one `claude -p "/implement-bead"` process per bead and stops when the
  planned queue is dry.
- `implement-bead` ends after one bead instead of going again. Its "queue is dry, stop" rule and its
  "clean up the worktree on every exit" rule already fit; this is mostly deleting a sentence.
- Say in the skill that the loop is external, so a future reader does not restore the inner loop.

## Out of scope

- Any change to what the implementer does within a bead: claiming, TDD, review, merge, cleanup.
- The planning role, which has the same shape but is interactive by design and is not looped.
- Running several implementers at once. The script runs one; several are several invocations.
acceptance_criteria: A loop script runs one claude process per bead and exits when nothing planned is ready; implement-bead no longer instructs the session to take another bead and says the loop is external; the navigator has reviewed and merged the change
notes:
Scope extended by the navigator mid-implementation (2026-08-13): the loop takes a mandatory name,
passed to each session as --remote-control <name> so a running implementer can be reached remotely
and two loops are told apart; and implementation sessions started by hand ask the navigator for /rc,
since an agent cannot enable Remote Control itself (/rc is a built-in command, not a skill).

Measured while wiring it: `claude -p` accepts --remote-control despite the flag's help saying
"interactive", and the session appears in the peer list under the given name. A finished -p session
leaves the peer list when it exits, which is why the name is reused for every bead rather than
suffixed with a counter - at any moment the loop has exactly one session listed.
close_reason: Delivered in PR #156, then withdrawn and replaced by ah-6xq.9

title: Release still strands when the export goes stale during the gate
description:
## Summary

`pnpm run release` still strands a release, for the reason ah-7go's fix does not cover: with several
agents working the backlog, the bead export goes stale *repeatedly*, so settling it once before the
bump only narrows the window instead of closing it. The v0.5.3 release failed exactly as v0.5.2 did
and had to be finished by hand.

The same race makes any push to main from an agent's worktree fail an unpredictable number of times;
tidying merged branches took four attempts on 2026-08-13.

## What happened on v0.5.3

The script did everything ah-7go asked of it, in order, and still ended stranded:

1. `settleExport` ran the gate, found the export stale, committed the refresh and **pushed it
   cleanly** (`acf6fd3..a9b25cc`).
2. The whole local gate passed: lint, typecheck, unit tests, rustfmt, clippy, Rust suite.
3. Both manifests were written and committed as `Release v0.5.3`.
4. `git push origin HEAD:main` fired the gate **again** - the export had gone stale during the gate -
   so it committed another refresh and aborted the push.
5. The script reported the failure and exited 1, before `git tag`.

End state: the version committed, nothing pushed, no tag. Recovering it by hand needed one `git push`
retry (the second attempt succeeded), then `git tag v0.5.3` and a tag push.

The window ah-7go's settle leaves open is the entire quality gate - minutes - and that is precisely
when other agents claim, heartbeat and close beads. A claim's `heartbeat_at` and `lease_expires_at`
are serialized into `.beads/issues.jsonl`, and a heartbeat lands about every minute per active claim,
so while any other agent holds a bead the export is close to always stale.

## What ah-7go did get right, and should be kept

- `settleExport` before the bump is still worth having: it keeps the release commit and its tag
  adjacent, and it is why step 1 above was cheap rather than another stranded state.
- `describeGitFailure` worked. The failure read `release: git push origin HEAD:main failed.` instead
  of the bare `execFileSync` stack trace that hid the cause on v0.5.2.

Neither needs redoing. This bead is the retry they were missing.

## Scope

- Retry the push in `scripts/release.ts` rather than dying on the first refusal. The gate's own
  contract is "run the push again", and one retry is what both manual recoveries needed. Bound the
  retries and report plainly when they are exhausted, so a genuine refusal - a rejected ref, a
  credential failure - is never mistaken for the gate and retried forever.
- Apply the same to the tag push, which runs the hook too.
- Decide, with the navigator, whether the volatile lease fields belong in the committed export at
  all. `heartbeat_at` and `lease_expires_at` describe who is holding a bead this minute, not what the
  backlog is; excluding them from the export comparison (or from the export) would make the gate
  settle for everyone, not only for releases. This is the root cause; the retry is the containment.
- The release must end tagged and pushed, or leave nothing behind. A run that dies after the bump
  should say what to do next, naming the commit and the tag that were not created.

## Out of scope

- Rewriting the export gate's abort-and-ask-again contract. A pre-push hook cannot amend the refs git
  has already computed, so the second push is inherent; what changes is who retries it.
- The `main` ruleset and its admin bypass.
- ah-vek, the worktree-anchored `cargoTargetDir` test, which is a separate failure of the same gate
  run.

## Validation

- A release run while another agent is actively claiming and closing beads ends tagged and pushed,
  with no manual recovery.
- Simulated: make the export stale between the settle and the push (touch the database, or stub the
  gate to fail once) and assert the script still completes. `scripts/releaseSupport.test.ts` already
  has the shape for this.
- A push that fails for a reason other than the gate is reported and not retried into a loop, pinned
  by a test.
- `pnpm run test:tooling` covers the retry logic.
design:
## Context

`pnpm run release` still strands a release. ah-7go's `settleExport` runs the export gate before the
bump, which is right and stays, but it only narrows the window: the gate runs again on the release's
own push, minutes later, and with other agents working the backlog the export has gone stale again
by then. v0.5.3 ended with the version committed, nothing pushed and no tag, recovered by hand.

**Measured, and this is the whole of the root cause.** Two exports taken either side of a single
`bd heartbeat`, compared field by field, differ in exactly two fields and nothing else:

    ah-r2e lease_expires_at '2026-08-13T11:18:42Z' -> '2026-08-13T11:19:48Z'
    ah-r2e heartbeat_at     '2026-08-13T11:13:42Z' -> '2026-08-13T11:14:48Z'

`updated_at` does **not** move. So the export churns once a minute per active claim, purely from
liveness data that says who is holding a bead this minute rather than what the backlog is — and
because the gate compares the export byte for byte, every push to main during another agent's claim
meets a refresh. That is also why tidying merged branches took four pushes on 2026-08-13; the
release is only the loudest victim.

`bd export` has no field filter (`--all`, `--scrub`, `--include-*`, `--exclude-owner` and nothing
else), so the normalization has to live in the gate.

When this lands: pushes to main stop being a lottery for everyone, and a release that still meets a
genuine refusal says what it did not do instead of dying mid-way.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

- **`scripts/beadsExportGate.ts`** — the root-cause fix.
  - New exported pure `stableExport(text: string): string`: JSONL in, JSONL out, with
    `heartbeat_at` and `lease_expires_at` removed from each record. A line that will not parse is
    passed through untouched. This function must never throw — the file's own promise is that the
    gate is a convenience that never blocks a push.
  - `decideGate` compares `stableExport(fresh)` against `stableExport(committed)`. **Both sides**,
    which matters for more than symmetry: both then go through the same `JSON.parse` →
    `JSON.stringify` round trip, so any difference in how bd and Node spell the same object (key
    order, unicode escaping, number formatting) cancels instead of showing up as a permanent false
    diff on the first run.
  - A refresh writes `stableExport(fresh)`, so what lands in the file is what the next comparison
    expects.
  - Keep the shape: `decideGate` stays the pure decision, `inspect` stays the gathering, `runGate`
    stays the doing. Normalizing inside `decideGate` keeps every case testable without git.
  - Export the retry sentinel (see below) as a named constant beside `REFRESH_MESSAGE`, and build
    the existing stderr message from it.
- **`scripts/releaseSupport.ts`** — the containment. Two new pure functions beside `settleStep`,
  `settleExport` and `describeGitFailure`, all of which stay as they are:
  - `isGateAbort(output: string): boolean` — whether a failed push is the gate asking for another
    push, matched on the constant imported from `beadsExportGate.ts`.
  - `recoveryAdvice(state): string[]` — given what did and did not happen (commit pushed? tag
    created? tag pushed?), the lines a human needs to finish by hand, naming the actual commands.
  - `pushWithRetry(push: () => { ok: boolean; output: string }, attempts: number)` — retries only
    while `isGateAbort` holds, and reports plainly when the attempts run out. Injected push, so it
    is unit-testable without git or a remote.
- **`scripts/release.ts`** — use them. Today `git()` calls `fail()`, which `process.exit`s, so no
  caller can ever see a failure; add a non-fatal `tryGit` returning `{ ok, output }` (reusing
  `describeGitFailure` for the text) and route the three pushes — the settle push, the version-commit
  push, the tag push — through `pushWithRetry`. On exhaustion, print `recoveryAdvice` and exit 1.
- **`scripts/beadsExportGate.test.ts`**, **`scripts/releaseSupport.test.ts`** — extended. The
  temp-repo harness at the bottom of the gate's test file (`setUpRepository`, the stub `bd`, the
  installed hook) is what proves the normalization end to end; reuse it rather than building another.

## Increments

1. **Stop the churn.** RED: `stableExport strips the lease fields and leaves everything else` in
   `beadsExportGate.test.ts`. GREEN: the function.
2. **Wire it into the decision.** RED: `decideGate lets a push through when only the lease fields
   moved` — two exports differing solely in `heartbeat_at`/`lease_expires_at`, expecting
   `{ kind: "proceed", reason: "up-to-date" }`. GREEN: normalize both sides in `decideGate`, and
   write the normalized text on refresh.
3. **Prove it against git.** RED: a temp-repo case in `the gate as a pre-push hook` where the stub
   `bd` exports the committed backlog with a moved heartbeat only — the push must succeed first
   time, with no refresh commit. GREEN: nothing new if 1 and 2 were honest.
4. **Retry the push.** RED: `pushWithRetry retries a gate abort and succeeds on the second attempt`.
   GREEN: `isGateAbort`, the constant exported from the gate, and `pushWithRetry`.
5. **Do not retry a real refusal.** RED: `pushWithRetry reports a rejected ref once, without
   retrying` — one attempt, and the message carries git's own words. GREEN: falls out of 4 if the
   predicate is written as "retry only on the sentinel" rather than "retry unless recognised".
6. **Never strand silently.** RED: `recoveryAdvice names the tag that was not pushed` and its
   siblings for the two earlier states. GREEN: the function, then `release.ts` calling it, and
   `tryGit`.

## The test plan

Suite: `pnpm run test:tooling`. It is the only one that covers `scripts/`, and nothing here touches
the application, so the browser suites are irrelevant to this bead.

`scripts/beadsExportGate.test.ts`:
- `stableExport strips the lease fields and leaves everything else` — one record with both fields
  and a full spread of the others; every other key survives, in order.
- `stableExport leaves a line it cannot parse alone` — a truncated line stays byte-identical. The
  gate must not be able to corrupt the export while trying to tidy it.
- `stableExport handles an empty export and a file with no trailing newline` — both round-trip
  unchanged, so an empty database does not produce a diff against an empty file.
- `decideGate lets a push through when only the lease fields moved` — the regression this bead is
  named for.
- `decideGate still refreshes when a bead actually changed` — the same pair, plus a changed
  `status`. Without this, the fix could be "compare nothing" and still pass.
- The temp-repo case from increment 3: `passes first time when only a heartbeat moved`, asserting
  status 0, no `refresh the issues export` in the output, and `git log` unchanged.
- Every existing case stays.

`scripts/releaseSupport.test.ts`:
- `isGateAbort recognises the gate's own words` — built from the exported constant, not from a
  hand-typed copy.
- `isGateAbort does not claim a rejected ref` — `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)`.
- `pushWithRetry retries a gate abort and succeeds on the second attempt` — the injected push
  counts its calls; exactly two.
- `pushWithRetry reports a rejected ref once, without retrying` — exactly one call, and the report
  carries git's text.
- `pushWithRetry gives up after the bound and says so` — a push that aborts for ever calls exactly
  the bound, and the message says the gate kept refreshing.
- `recoveryAdvice` — three cases: nothing pushed; commit pushed, no tag; tag made, not pushed. Each
  names the exact commands, including the version, so the lines can be pasted.

Not tested automatically, by choice: `release.ts` end to end. It cuts a real release; the pieces it
composes are all pure and covered above.

## User-facing decisions

None. This is release tooling and a pre-push hook; the application has no part in it.

Two judgements taken here rather than left to the implementer, both recorded so they are not
re-opened mid-implementation:

- **The volatile lease fields leave the committed export**, and the comparison normalizes both
  sides. The bead's description raises this as a question; the measurement above answers it. They
  are per-minute liveness of a claim on one machine, `bd export` is explicitly not a backup (bd's
  own help says so, and points at `bd backup` for that), and claim state travels between agents by
  `bd dolt push` rather than through this file. Nothing reads them from the export.
- **Three attempts**, not one retry and not unbounded. One refresh is what both manual recoveries
  needed, but the export can go stale again between two attempts, and an unbounded loop against a
  genuinely refusing remote is worse than a clear failure.

## Out of scope

- The gate's abort-and-ask-again contract. A pre-push hook cannot amend refs git has already
  computed, so the second push is inherent; what changes is who runs it.
- `settleExport` and `describeGitFailure`. Both worked on v0.5.3 and are kept as they are.
- The `main` ruleset and its admin bypass.
- ah-vek, the worktree-anchored `cargoTargetDir` test — a separate failure of the same gate run.
- Retrying anything other than a push. The release's checks, commit and tag stay single-shot.
- Making `bd` itself export fewer fields. The normalization lives in this repository's gate.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run test:tooling
pnpm run check
```

Then, by hand, the thing no unit test can reach:

```bash
bd heartbeat <a bead you hold>     # churn the export the way another agent would
git push origin HEAD:main          # must succeed first time, with no refresh commit
git log --oneline -1               # and must not have grown a "refresh the issues export"
pnpm run release maintenance --dry-run
```

Human-only, and the real acceptance: the next actual release ends tagged and pushed with no manual
recovery. Do not cut a release to test this bead.

## Known traps

- **The retry matcher and the gate's message must not drift.** The gate's line is
  `beads: nothing was pushed - run the push again to send it along.` If `release.ts` matches a
  hand-typed copy, rewording the gate silently disarms the retry and the next release strands
  exactly as v0.5.3 did — with all tests green. Export one constant from `beadsExportGate.ts`, build
  the stderr message from it, and match on it. That is why increment 4 depends on the constant.
- **`git()` in `release.ts` exits the process.** It calls `fail()`, so a retry wrapped around it can
  never run — the first refusal takes the whole script down. A non-fatal variant is needed before
  any retry is possible; writing the retry first and finding this out afterwards is the likely
  order of discovery.
- **Do not reach for `--no-verify`.** It makes the symptom vanish by pushing a stale export and
  skipping every other hook, and it is not what this bead is for.
- **`stableExport` must never throw.** The gate's stated promise is that a convenience never blocks
  a push. A parse failure on one line must leave that line alone and carry on, not take the hook
  down — and the test for it exists so nobody "simplifies" the try/catch away.
- **Normalize both sides, or the first run rewrites the file for nothing.** bd's serialization and
  Node's `JSON.stringify` need not agree byte for byte; normalizing only the fresh side compares
  Node's spelling against bd's and can differ permanently.
- **The lease fields are sparse.** Only a bead currently claimed carries them — one line in 33 today
  — so a test fixture built from a random export may contain none at all and pass while asserting
  nothing. Build the fixture explicitly.
- **`updated_at` is not the culprit** and must keep being compared. Measured: a heartbeat leaves it
  alone. Stripping it too would hide real edits.
- **Do not `git checkout main`** — another agent usually holds it in a worktree. Branch from
  `origin/main` after `git fetch origin main`.
- **The temp-repo tests are macOS-sensitive**: `/tmp` is a symlink to `/private/tmp`, so compare git
  output against git output, as `beadsExportGate.test.ts` already carefully does.
- **This bead and ah-vek both touch `scripts/`** but no file in common. If ah-vek lands first,
  `pnpm test` runs its legs through a runner; `release.ts` invokes `pnpm -r run test` directly and
  is unaffected either way.
acceptance_criteria: A release run while another agent is claiming and closing beads ends with the version commit pushed and the tag pushed, without manual recovery; the push is retried on the export gate's abort and not on a genuine refusal, pinned by a test; a run that still cannot finish names the commit and tag it did not create

title: Release script dies on the export gate's aborted push
description:
## Summary

`pnpm run release <bump>` strands the release: it commits the version bump and then dies before
tagging, leaving the two manifests at the new version with no tag and nothing pushed. This happened
to v0.5.2, which sat committed-but-untagged on local main until the tag was pushed by hand.

## Problem

The release script and the bead export gate have contradictory contracts, and the release script
loses.

`scripts/beadsExportGate.ts` runs from `.beads/hooks/pre-push`. On main, when the committed
`.beads/issues.jsonl` differs from a fresh export, it commits the refresh on its own and returns 1
to abort the push, printing "nothing was pushed - run the push again". A pre-push hook cannot amend
the refs git has already computed, so that second push is the design, not a failure.

`scripts/release.ts` does not push again. Its `git()` helper (`release.ts:44`) calls `execFileSync`
with piped stdio, so the aborted push throws an uncaught exception and the gate's explanation is
swallowed into a buffer nobody reads. The script dies at `release.ts:182`, before `git tag`
(`release.ts:187`).

Evidence from the v0.5.2 attempt, reflog timestamps to the second:

- `02:14:18` `Release v0.5.2` — the release script's commit
- `02:14:20` `chore(beads): refresh the issues export` — the gate's commit, two seconds later
- no `v0.5.2` tag, nothing pushed

This recurs on essentially every release. Cutting a release follows bead work — claim, update,
close — so the export is stale by the time the release commit lands. v0.5.1 got through only
because the export happened to be current.

Re-running after the failure makes it worse rather than resuming: the manifests are clean at the
already-bumped version, so a second `release maintenance` bumps again and the stranded version is
never released.

Two consequences worth designing around rather than fighting:

- The gate's commit always lands between the release commit and the tag, so the tag can never sit
  on the `Release vX` commit while the gate runs after the bump.
- The release script has no test coverage at all, unlike `beadsExportGate.ts` and `diskPreflight.ts`
  which are both tested.

## Scope

- Make `pnpm run release` survive the export gate so a release run ends tagged and pushed.
- Make git failures inside the release script legible instead of an uncaught `execFileSync` stack
  trace — a rejected push, a hook that stood in the way, a missing credential should each say so.
- Cover the new behaviour with tests, in the shape `beadsExportGate.ts` and `diskPreflight.ts`
  already use: the decision logic split from the doing, so the cases are testable without pushing.

Two approaches, to be decided with the navigator when the bead is worked:

1. Retry the push once. The gate is a no-op the second time. Smallest change; leaves the tag on the
   gate's commit.
2. Push once before the bump, so the gate fires while nothing is at stake, and the release commit
   and its tag stay adjacent. Slightly more moving parts, better end state.

## Out of scope

- Changing the export gate's behaviour. Its "push again" contract is deliberate and documented; the
  release script is what must accommodate it.
- The `main` ruleset (10 required status checks, admin-only bypass). It is a separate concern that
  will reject this same push for a non-admin token, but it is not what broke v0.5.2.
- Any rework of the release GitHub workflow itself.

## Validation

- `pnpm run release maintenance --dry-run` with a deliberately stale `.beads/issues.jsonl` on main:
  the run completes rather than dying at the push.
- A full release run from main with a stale export ends with the tag pushed and origin/main
  carrying both the release commit and the gate's refresh commit.
- `pnpm run test:tooling` covers the new logic.
- The failure paths report their cause: point the script at an unpushable remote and confirm the
  message names the push rather than printing a stack trace.
acceptance_criteria: A release run from main with a stale .beads/issues.jsonl ends with the version commit pushed and the tag pushed, rather than stopping at the commit; a git failure inside release.ts reports what failed instead of an uncaught execFileSync stack trace; the new logic is covered by tests under pnpm run test:tooling

title: cargoTargetDir's worktree check fails whenever pnpm check runs from a worktree
description:
`scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts` derives the repository root from its own file location (`scripts/..`). Run from a git worktree that is what it gets - `.claude/worktrees/<name>` - so `git worktree list` then reports the main checkout and every sibling worktree as strays, and the test fails:

    expected [ '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud',
               '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/.claude/worktrees/pr75' ] to deeply equal []

CI never sees it, because a CI checkout has no worktrees. It bites locally, and it bites in the one workflow this repository actually prescribes: CLAUDE.md has agents work in `.claude/worktrees/`, where `pnpm check` now stops at `pnpm test` before it reaches the smoke suite. Hit while merging ah-ebv (#144); the whole remaining gate had to be run by hand, step by step.

The property the test is defending is right - a worktree outside the repository silently gets its own target directory and its own empty bead database. It is the anchor that is wrong: the root should come from git (`git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`, then up one from `.git`) rather than from where the test file happens to sit, so the check asks the same question wherever it is run from.

## Validation

- `pnpm run test:tooling` passes from a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` and from the main checkout alike.
- A control: a worktree created outside the repository is still reported as a stray, so the test has not simply been widened into always passing.
design:
## Context

`scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts` guards a real property: every git worktree must sit inside the
repository, because that is what puts it under `.cargo/config.toml` and gives it the one shared
`target/` (and the one shared bead database). The property is right; the anchor is wrong. The test
derives the repository root from its own file location — `resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), "..")`
— so when `pnpm run test:tooling` runs from a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<name>`, "the
repository" is that worktree, and `git worktree list` then reports the main checkout and every
sibling worktree as strays:

    expected [ '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud',
               '/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/.claude/worktrees/pr75' ] to deeply equal []

CI never sees it — a CI checkout has no worktrees — but it fires in the one workflow this repository
prescribes, where agents work in `.claude/worktrees/`.

The second cost is worse than the noise. `pnpm test` is an `&&` chain:

    pnpm -r run test && pnpm run test:tooling && cargo test --workspace

`test:tooling` is the middle link, so a spurious failure there means `cargo test --workspace` never
runs at all. An agent who reads it as "unrelated tooling test" and moves on has skipped 576 Rust
tests while believing the gate covered them. On ah-ctf they only ran because someone noticed the
short-circuit by hand.

When this lands: `pnpm run test:tooling` asks the same question wherever it is run from, and
`pnpm test` can no longer hide whether a suite ran.

## Files to change, and what to reuse

- **`scripts/cargoTargetDir.ts`** — new. Today the check lives entirely inside the test, which is why
  it cannot be exercised anywhere but against the real repository. Extract two things:
  - `repositoryRoot(cwd: string): string` — `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir`
    from `cwd`, then one directory up from the returned `.git`. Verified by hand at git 2.54: from
    the main checkout it answers `/Users/henrikku/repos/atlantis-hud/.git`, and from
    `.claude/worktrees/task` it answers the same path — that identity is the whole fix.
    Do **not** use `--show-toplevel`, which answers the worktree in a worktree.
  - `strayWorktrees(porcelain: string, root: string): string[]` — pure, taking the raw text of
    `git worktree list --porcelain`. Move the existing parsing (`/^worktree (.+)$/gmu`), the
    `normalize` helper, the `AGENT_WORKSPACES = ".claude"` constant and the trailing-separator guard
    across unchanged; they are all correct, and the `.claude-old` reasoning in the comment must
    travel with the code.
- **`scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts`** — rewritten around the module. Keep all three existing
  assertions (config exists, `target-dir` is `"target"`, the path is relative and has no `~`) and
  their comments; only their `REPO` changes.
- **`scripts/runSuites.ts`** — new; the three-leg runner. Follow the shape of `scripts/diskPreflight.ts`
  and `scripts/beadsExportGate.ts`: a pure decision function plus a thin `main` guarded by the
  `process.argv[1] !== undefined && resolve(process.argv[1]) === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)`
  idiom those two already use.
- **`scripts/runSuites.test.ts`** — new.
- **`package.json`** — `"test"` becomes `tsx scripts/runSuites.ts`. The leg commands move into the
  script. `test:tooling` stays as its own script: CI calls it directly (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:134`).
- **`README.md`** (the "Check and test" section around line 129) — one sentence that `pnpm run test`
  runs all three suites and reports each, rather than stopping at the first.

Nothing else anchors on `scripts/..` for the repository: `diskPreflight.test.ts`, `gateLock.test.ts`
and `beadsExportGate.test.ts` use `HERE` only to locate `tsx` and a script beside them, which is
correct wherever it runs.

## Increments

Each opens with the named test failing.

1. **Extract the check, no behaviour change.**
   RED: `cargoTargetDir.test.ts` imports `strayWorktrees` from `./cargoTargetDir`, which does not
   exist. GREEN: the module, with the parsing and the guard moved across; the real-repository test
   still calls it with the old file-derived root, so it still fails in a worktree. That is expected
   at this step and fixed in 2.

2. **Anchor the root in git.**
   RED: `repositoryRoot answers the same path from a worktree as from the checkout it belongs to` —
   a throwaway repository with a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`, asserting one path from both.
   GREEN: `repositoryRoot`, then `cargoTargetDir.test.ts` uses `repositoryRoot(HERE)` in place of
   `resolve(HERE, "..")`. The whole tooling suite now passes from a worktree.

3. **The control, so the check has not been widened into always passing.**
   RED: `reports a worktree outside the repository as a stray` — a throwaway repository with two
   worktrees, one under `.claude/worktrees/` and one in a sibling temp directory; only the second is
   returned. GREEN: nothing to write if 1 and 2 were done honestly; if it passes on the first run,
   say so in the commit rather than inventing a change.

4. **The suite runner.**
   RED: `runSuites.test.ts` expects `summarize` from `./runSuites`. GREEN: `summarize`, then the
   runner around it, then `package.json` and the README sentence. The output shape to follow:

       $ pnpm test
       ...
       suites: packages PASS  tooling FAIL  cargo PASS
       1 of 3 suites failed: tooling

   The legs run sequentially in the order above, each with inherited stdio, and every leg runs
   whatever the ones before it did. The accepted cost is that a failing local run is now slower,
   since a broken leg no longer stops the others — that is the trade this bead is making on
   purpose, and it is what stops a failure in one suite from hiding whether the others ran.

Keep 1–3 and 4 as separate commits under the one bead ID; they are one PR.

## The test plan

Suites: `pnpm run test:tooling` is the one that must run, and it must be run **twice** — once from
the main checkout and once from a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/`. Running it in one place only
is how this bug survived. `pnpm run check` at the end.

`scripts/cargoTargetDir.test.ts`:
- the three existing config assertions, unchanged in substance.
- `keeps the worktrees inside the repository` — as now, but rooted at `repositoryRoot(HERE)`.
- `strayWorktrees` unit table, pure, no git: the root alone is not a stray; a path under
  `<root>/.claude/worktrees/x` is not; `<root>/.claude-old/x` **is** (the trailing-separator guard);
  a path outside the root is; a path spelled with backslashes normalizes (the existing `normalize`
  comment says git reports forward slashes on Windows too — pin that the comparison is about the
  path, not the platform).
- `repositoryRoot answers the same path from a worktree as from the checkout it belongs to` —
  throwaway repository, as increment 2.
- `reports a worktree outside the repository as a stray` — throwaway repository, as increment 3.
  This is the acceptance criterion that the check was not simply widened.

`scripts/runSuites.test.ts` — `summarize` is pure, so state the cases plainly:
- all three legs pass → exit 0, and the summary names all three as passing.
- the middle leg fails → exit non-zero, the summary names `tooling` as the failure **and** shows that
  `cargo` still ran. This is the regression under test; without the second half the change is
  invisible.
- two legs fail → both named, exit non-zero.

For the throwaway repositories, copy the pattern from `beadsExportGate.test.ts` (`mkdtempSync`,
`git init`, a seed commit, an inner `git()` helper). They need `git worktree add`, which requires a
commit, and a `user.email`/`user.name` set locally.

## User-facing decisions

None. This bead touches the repository's own tooling — a vitest suite, a package script and the
README — and nothing the application's users ever see. No mockup was built and none is committed.

The one judgement call worth recording, taken at planning rather than left to the implementer:
`pnpm test` runs all three legs instead of stopping at the first failure. The `&&` chain is what
turned this bug into a silently skipped Rust suite, and fixing the anchor alone would leave the same
trap armed for the next spurious failure. The shape is fixed in increment 4; do not re-litigate it.

## Out of scope

- `pnpm run check` stays an `&&` chain. Only `test` changes; making the whole gate collect failures
  is a different question and a different bead.
- CI is untouched. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` invokes `test:tooling`, `test:pwa` and the rest as
  separate steps and never calls `pnpm run test`, so it already reports every suite independently.
- No change to `.cargo/config.toml` or to what `target-dir` is. The configuration is right; only the
  test's idea of where the repository is was wrong.
- Not a general "run legs in parallel" runner. Sequential, so the output stays readable and cargo and
  vitest do not contend.
- No change to `bd`'s own database-location behaviour, mentioned in the test comment as the other
  thing a stray worktree breaks.

## Validation

```bash
pnpm run test:tooling                                   # from the main checkout
git -C <repo> worktree list                             # confirm at least one worktree exists first
(cd <repo>/.claude/worktrees/<name> && pnpm run test:tooling)   # the case that fails today
pnpm run check
```

The control the acceptance criteria ask for is the automated test from increment 3; no manual
outside-worktree creation is needed.

Human-only, and worth doing once before the PR: break a tooling test on purpose, run `pnpm test`,
and confirm the Rust suite still ran and the summary names the failing leg. That is the whole point
of increment 4 and no unit test proves it end to end.

## Known traps

- **`/tmp` is a symlink to `/private/tmp` on macOS.** `mkdtempSync` hands back one spelling and git
  hands back the other, so a temp-repo test comparing a git answer against a constructed path fails
  for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. `realpathSync` both sides before comparing.
  `beadsExportGate.test.ts` sidesteps this by only ever comparing git output against git output;
  these tests cannot, since the point is that `repositoryRoot` agrees with a known path.
- **`git rev-parse --path-format=absolute` needs git ≥ 2.31.** Fine here (2.54) and on CI, but it is
  the reason not to hand-roll the relative form.
- **`--show-toplevel` is the wrong question.** In a worktree it answers the worktree, which is exactly
  the bug being fixed. It must be `--git-common-dir`, and the root is one level up from it.
- **The main checkout is often on a detached HEAD** (it is right now) and several worktrees exist in
  parallel. `git worktree list --porcelain` handles that; anything that assumes a branch does not.
- **Never `git checkout main`.** Another agent usually holds main in a worktree and the checkout
  fails. Branch from `origin/main` after `git fetch origin main`.
- **`pnpm -r run test` must not include the workspace root**, or `pnpm test` recurses into itself for
  ever once `test` points at the runner. `-r` excludes the root by default and
  `pnpm-workspace.yaml` lists only `apps/*` and `packages/*` — leave it that way and never add
  `--include-workspace-root` to that leg.
- **The runner must inherit stdio and must exit non-zero if any leg failed.** `pnpm run check`
  depends on that exit code; a runner that summarises nicely and exits 0 turns the whole gate green
  while tests fail.
- **Do not create worktrees in the real repository from a test.** Every worktree the new tests make
  lives in its own temp repository, and is removed with the temp directory.
- **Do not weaken the stray check to make it pass.** The property is the point; the anchor was the
  bug. Increment 3 exists to prove that distinction, so it must fail if `strayWorktrees` is loosened.
acceptance_criteria:
pnpm run test:tooling passes when run from a worktree under .claude/worktrees/, and from the main checkout.
The repository root is taken from git rather than from the test file's own path.
A worktree genuinely outside the repository still fails the check, pinned by a test.
notes:
Raised to P1 on 2026-08-13 after hitting it a second time, while gating ah-ctf (#149).

What the description does not yet record, and what makes this worse than a noisy check: pnpm run test is an && chain -

  pnpm -r run test && pnpm run test:tooling && cargo test --workspace

test:tooling is the failing link, so cargo test --workspace never runs at all. An agent who reads the failure as 'unrelated tooling test' and moves on has silently skipped the entire Rust suite while believing the gate covered it. On ah-ctf the 576 Rust tests only ran because the short-circuit was noticed and cargo test was invoked separately.

So the cost is not only the manual gate the description mentions. It is a gate that looks broader than it is, in the exact direction - Rust - that the TypeScript suites cannot cover. Worth considering as part of the fix whether the chain should keep going and report every failure rather than stopping at the first.

title: Instructions for the two agent roles
description:
Two documents have to agree before either skill ships, because CLAUDE.md is always loaded and a skill that contradicts it resolves unpredictably - some sessions stall waiting for the navigator, some merge and are in violation.

- The Four Eye Principle in .github/copilot-instructions.md currently says no automatic merging is allowed and that the navigator must approve every PR. It is amended to name the Copilot reviewer as the second pair of eyes for bead-implemented PRs, with its conditions: every mandatory plan section present, every review thread resolved against the final head, and every check green.
- The beads-workflow skill gains the planned / human / needs-ui-decision lifecycle and its two atomic pickups.
- The never-reclaim rule, written when nothing heartbeated, is narrowed: a scoped bd reclaim --older-than 15m --label planned is allowed now that agents heartbeat, paired with pruning the dead agent's worktree.
acceptance_criteria:
CLAUDE.md and the beads-workflow skill agree with each other and with the two new skills on merging, claiming and reclaiming.
The label lifecycle is documented in one place and referenced from the others.
The narrowed reclaim rule says what makes a stale lease meaningful now and what it still does not license.

title: The plan-bead and implement-bead skills
description:
The two skills themselves: .claude/skills/plan-bead/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/implement-bead/SKILL.md, invoked as /plan-bead and /implement-bead in their own sessions. Committed automatically under the existing .gitignore rule that shares .claude/skills/.

The planner states its required model (Fable, else Opus, high effort) and declines to run on anything else - a skill cannot set the session model, but it can refuse. It claims with bd ready --exclude-label planned --claim, researches, takes architecture decisions itself, discusses every UI decision with the navigator over self-contained HTML mockups, writes the plan to the design field, labels it planned and unclaims.

The implementer claims with bd ready --label planned --claim, works in .claude/worktrees/<bead-id>, runs TDD under standing pre-approval, and waits for a Copilot review whose commit.oid equals the current head - never for an approval, which never comes.
acceptance_criteria:
Both skills exist, are invocable as /plan-bead and /implement-bead, and are committed.
The planner refuses to run on the wrong model and never plans a UI bead unattended.
The implementer refuses a plan missing a mandatory section and hands the bead back in one command.
The review wait keys on commit.oid matching the head SHA, and re-requests review after pushing fixes.
notes:
Traps for the implement-bead skill, found by running the loop:

1. The smoke suite rebuilds apps/web/dist with ATLANTIS_PWA_DISABLE=1, so running test:pwa after test:smoke without rebuilding fails with page timeouts and no service worker. pnpm check orders it build:web then test:pwa for exactly this reason. An agent that meets this unattended will plausibly go and 'fix' the service worker.

2. Never arm 'gh pr merge --auto' before the review round is closed. Auto-merge fires on green checks alone: it does not wait for a review, and it races any fix pushed afterwards. On #142 it merged the pre-review head and --delete-branch then removed the branch carrying the fixes, which survived only in the local object store.

3. Expect BEHIND on nearly every merge. With the strict up-to-date rule and several agents merging, a PR that sat through one review round is usually behind main, and each rebase costs a full CI cycle. Rebase, re-run the local gate, force-with-lease.

4. Copilot reviews roughly four PRs in five, sometimes minutes late, and never approves - every review is COMMENTED. Wait on a review whose commit.oid equals the current head, re-request after every push, and bound the wait.
Merge discipline, decided with the navigator after four of five PRs each needed an extra rebase and full CI cycle purely because another agent merged during review:

Keep the strict branches-up-to-date rule and rebase every time. A green gate on a stale tree is evidence about a tree that will never exist, and two agents changing the same function compatibly - both green, broken on main - is exactly what the rule catches. No merge queue for now.

The skill must state the cost plainly rather than let each agent rediscover it: expect BEHIND on most merges, budget a rebase plus a full CI cycle per review round, and never treat the rebase as optional. Revisit if the agent count grows past three or so.

title: Protect main so red or stale work cannot merge
description:
gh api reports main is not protected: no ruleset, no required checks, and allow_auto_merge is false. So 'CI must be green' would be enforced only by an agent reading gh pr checks correctly - and every known misreading (a pending check taken as passed, a queued job ignored, a green-but-stale branch) lands straight on main with no backstop. This is the single largest false-green lever in the harness.

A ruleset on main requires the CI job names with branches-up-to-date, auto-merge is enabled, and the agent's merge step becomes gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch --auto: GitHub then owns waiting, ordering and staleness, and the agent's attempt budget becomes a give-up rule rather than a merge-permission rule.

The navigator is a bypass actor. This is a settings change on a live repository and needs the navigator to make it or to approve the exact gh api calls.
acceptance_criteria:
A ruleset on main requires the CI job names and branches to be up to date.
Auto-merge is enabled on the repository.
The navigator is a bypass actor; agent PRs are not exempt.
A deliberately red PR cannot be merged by the documented agent command.
notes: Amended after review with the navigator: a bypass actor was added (RepositoryRole 5, admin, bypass_mode always). Verified by probe - a direct push to main is now permitted with a '10 of 10 required status checks are expected' warning rather than declined. The trade is explicit: agents authenticate with the navigator's token and hold admin, so they inherit the bypass. The ruleset therefore stops accidents (red or stale merges through the PR path, force-pushes, branch deletion) but is not a hard guarantee against an agent that merges deliberately. That guarantee, if wanted later, needs a separate identity for agents.
close_reason: Ruleset 20771276 active on main: 10 required checks, strict up-to-date, no bypass; auto-merge enabled. Verified by a rejected direct push.

title: One cargo build directory, and a disk preflight
description:
There is no .cargo/config.toml, so every git worktree builds its own target tree: 10G + 2.7G + 5.8G for one repository, on a disk that was at 100% capacity with 2.0 GiB free when this was found. Each further implementation agent adds another 3-6 GB, and cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets is the biggest of them.

The failure mode is an ENOSPC part-way through a build, which surfaces as a strange linker or codegen error that an agent will try to fix in code.

A committed .cargo/config.toml points every worktree at one shared build directory outside the repo. The per-worktree target trees then become dead weight and can be removed. An implementation agent refuses to start a bead when free space is under a threshold, rather than discovering it mid-build.
acceptance_criteria:
A committed .cargo/config.toml sets a shared build.target-dir outside the repository.
The obsolete per-worktree target trees are removed and the space is measurably reclaimed.
The implement skill refuses to create a worktree below a stated free-space threshold, naming the real cause.

title: Per-agent ports for the smoke and PWA suites
description:
playwright.config.ts pins 4173/4174 and playwright.pwa.config.ts pins 4175. Concurrent agents collide.

The PWA config is the dangerous one: its preview command has no --strictPort, so a second agent's Vite quietly falls back to 4176 while Playwright's readiness probe hits 4175 and finds the FIRST agent's server. Every PWA test then passes against someone else's bundle. The smoke config is safe only by luck, because it does pass --strictPort.

Both configs take a port base from an env var, defaulting to today's numbers so a plain local run is unchanged, and --strictPort is added to the PWA preview so a collision is always loud.
acceptance_criteria:
Both configs derive their ports from an env-provided base, defaulting to 4173/4174/4175.
The PWA preview command passes --strictPort.
Port resolution is a pure function with tests under the tooling vitest config.
Two agents run test:smoke and test:pwa simultaneously and pass against their own bundles; breaking one worktree's source reddens only that agent's run.

title: Export gate stands aside off main
description:
scripts/beadsExportGate.ts writes the whole bead database into .beads/issues.jsonl on every branch it runs on. Two agents' PRs therefore carry complete backlog snapshots taken at different moments, and whichever merges last silently reverts every close, claim, label and plan recorded in between. Git usually will not even conflict, because each side rewrote a different subset of the one-line-per-bead file.

The gate becomes a main-only obligation: on any other branch it stands aside, exactly as it already does when bd is missing or node_modules are absent. main is refreshed by the planner's own pushes and by a post-merge refresh.

This is the highest-probability silent-wrong-result in the harness, and it gets worse once plans live in the design field.
acceptance_criteria:
runGate proceeds without exporting when the current branch is not main.
The existing stand-aside idiom and its tests are followed rather than a new mechanism.
Two branches, each pushed after a bead change and merged in turn, leave the first branch's bead state intact - demonstrated, not assumed.

title: Planner and implementer agent harness
description:
